---
title: "Figure 5.2: Real Exports Growth"
---

![Python: `python/fig-5-2.py`](../images/python/fig-5-2.png)

Quarterly growth of real exports, year over year, for the United States,
Canada, LA7 and CAPDR, compared with the growth of world trade volume. The
lines cross zero several times, so the zero line matters for reading the
chart: it separates growth from contraction.

**Nothing new in this chart.** It combines quarters as categories ([Figure
1.1](fig-1-1.qmd)) with an axis line at zero ([Figure 2.1](fig-2-1.qmd)). It
is a good one to read without help, as a check. Try to explain each line of
the script to yourself before reading the explanation below.

## The data

Sheet `data`, 10 rows:

| category | USA | CAN | LA7 | CAPDR | World trade volume |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 2024Q1 | 2.27 | 1.83 | 1.12 | 0.80 | -0.13 |

The categories are quarters written as text (`2024Q1`, ...), and there is
one column per line.

## The script

### Colours and frame

```python
series_colours = {
    "USA": "#0868A4",
    "CAN": "#444444",
    "LA7": "#62317D",
    "CAPDR": "#C75B0A",
    "World trade volume": "#00A6A6",
}
```

The usual REO colours for the four economies, and teal for world trade.

`new_chart()` gets `bottom_gap=0.62`, about twice the usual space below the
plot, because the quarter labels are written vertically.

### The drawing

```python
x = np.arange(len(data))

# The x-axis is drawn at zero, with short tick marks pointing up; the
# quarter labels stay at the bottom of the chart.
ax.axhline(0, color="black", linewidth=0.8)
ax.vlines(x, 0, 0.22, color="black", linewidth=0.6)

for series, colour in series_colours.items():
    ax.plot(x, data[series], color=colour, linewidth=1.8,
            solid_capstyle="round", label=series)

ax.set_xticks(x, data["category"], rotation=90)
ax.set_xlim(-0.5, len(data) - 0.5)
ax.spines["bottom"].set_visible(False)
ax.tick_params(axis="x", length=0, pad=5)

set_y_scale(ax, -6, 9, 3)
ax.tick_params(axis="y", length=2.3)

ax.legend(loc="lower left", bbox_to_anchor=(0.03, 0.02), handlelength=3.0,
          labelspacing=0.05)
```

Step by step:

1. **Positions.** The quarters are text, so they are plotted at positions 0
   to 9, made by `np.arange(len(data))`. See [Categories as
   positions](../techniques.qmd#sec-categories).
2. **The axis line.** In the published chart, the horizontal axis crosses
   the y-axis at zero, in the middle of the plot, but the quarter labels are
   at the bottom (Excel's *Label position: Low*). matplotlib cannot split an
   axis like that, so the script draws the line at zero with
   `ax.axhline(0, ...)` and the tick marks with `ax.vlines(x, 0, 0.22,
   ...)`: one short vertical line at each quarter, from 0 to 0.22. The
   height is in data units. On a scale from -6 to 9, 0.22 is about 1.5
   percent of the height, which gives a short tick. See [An axis line at
   zero](../techniques.qmd#sec-axis-line).
3. **The lines.** The five series are drawn in the order of the
   dictionary, so world trade volume, last, lies on top. They are drawn
   after the axis line, so the lines cover it where they cross zero.
4. **The quarter labels.** `ax.set_xticks(x, labels, rotation=90)` writes
   them vertically under each position. The normal bottom axis line is
   hidden with `ax.spines["bottom"].set_visible(False)`, since the real axis
   line is now the one at zero. `length=0` removes the tick marks at the
   bottom, leaving only the labels.
5. **The x-limits** run half a step beyond the first and last quarter, as
   Excel leaves on a category axis.
6. **The y-scale.** It runs from -6 to 9 with a tick every 3, so zero is one
   of the ticks. When an axis line is drawn at zero, make sure zero falls on
   a tick; otherwise the line floats between labels. See [The
   y-scale](../chart-style.qmd#sec-y-scale).
7. **The legend.** It goes in the lower left, anchored at 3 percent from the
   left and 2 percent from the bottom of the plot. That corner is empty:
   the negative values only come later, in 2025 and 2026, when Canada's
   exports fall. `labelspacing=0.05` packs the five
   entries tightly so they fit. See [Legends](../techniques.qmd#sec-legends).

## Changing the chart

- **A new quarter.** Nothing in the script depends on the number of rows,
  so a longer data set works as it is. With more than about 16 quarters,
  label every second one, as in [Figure 2.4](fig-2-4.qmd).
- **A different y-range.** Choose limits that keep zero on a tick, for
  example `set_y_scale(ax, -8, 12, 4)`. Then check that the tick marks at
  zero are still short: on a wider scale, 0.22 gives a shorter tick, and you
  may want 0.3.
- **The legend elsewhere.** If new data fill the lower left, move it to the
  top with `loc="upper left", bbox_to_anchor=(0.03, 0.98)`.

## The complete script

The full `python/fig-5-2.py`, as it runs:

```` {.python filename="python/fig-5-2.py"}
"""Figure 5.2: Real Exports Growth."""
import numpy as np

from chart_style import new_chart, read_chart_data, save_chart, set_y_scale

STEM = "fig-5-2"

data = read_chart_data(STEM)

series_colours = {
    "USA": "#0868A4",
    "CAN": "#444444",
    "LA7": "#62317D",
    "CAPDR": "#C75B0A",
    "World trade volume": "#00A6A6",
}

fig, ax = new_chart(
    title="Real Exports Growth",
    subtitle="(Year-over-year percent change)",
    caption=(
        "Sources: CPB Netherlands Bureau for Economic Policy Analysis; Haver\n"
        "Analytics; national authorities; and IMF staff calculations.\n"
        "Note: Aggregates are purchasing-power-parity GDP-weighted averages.\n"
        "CAPDR = Central America, Panama, and the Dominican Republic; LA7 =\n"
        "Latin America 7 (Brazil, Chile, Colombia, Mexico, Paraguay, Peru,\n"
        "Uruguay)."
    ),
    left=0.3,
    right=0.2,
    bottom_gap=0.62,
)

x = np.arange(len(data))

# The x-axis is drawn at zero, with short tick marks pointing up; the
# quarter labels stay at the bottom of the chart.
ax.axhline(0, color="black", linewidth=0.8)
ax.vlines(x, 0, 0.22, color="black", linewidth=0.6)

for series, colour in series_colours.items():
    ax.plot(x, data[series], color=colour, linewidth=1.8,
            solid_capstyle="round", label=series)

ax.set_xticks(x, data["category"], rotation=90)
ax.set_xlim(-0.5, len(data) - 0.5)
ax.spines["bottom"].set_visible(False)
ax.tick_params(axis="x", length=0, pad=5)

set_y_scale(ax, -6, 9, 3)
ax.tick_params(axis="y", length=2.3)

ax.legend(loc="lower left", bbox_to_anchor=(0.03, 0.02), handlelength=3.0,
          labelspacing=0.05)

save_chart(fig, STEM)
````
